(a) Review Required.—
        (1) In general.—The Secretary of Defense shall require the Secretaries of the military departments to provide for review of decisions not to refer charges for trial by court-martial in cases where a sex-related offense has been alleged by a victim of the alleged offense. 
        (2) Specific review requirements.—As part of a review conducted pursuant to paragraph (1), the Secretary of a military department shall require that—
            (A) consideration be given to the victim’s statement provided during the course of the criminal investigation 
regarding the alleged sex-related offense perpetrated against the victim; and 
            (B) a determination be made whether the victim’s statement and views concerning disposition of the alleged sex-related offense were considered by the convening authority in making the referral decision.   
    (b) Sex-related Offense Defined.—In this section, the term “sex-related offense” means any of the following:
        (1) Rape or sexual assault under subsection (a) or (b) of section 920 of title 10, United States Code (article 120 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice). 
        (2) Forcible sodomy under section 925 of such title (article 125 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice). 
        (3) An attempt to commit an offense specified in paragraph (1) or (2) as punishable under section 880 of such title (article 80 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice).  
    (c) Review of Cases Not Referred to Court-martial Following Staff Judge Advocate Recommendation of Referral for Trial.—In any case where a staff judge advocate, pursuant to section 834 of title 10, United States Code (article 34 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice), recommends that charges of a sex-related offense be referred for trial by court-martial and the convening authority decides not to refer any charges to a court-martial, the convening authority shall forward the case file to the Secretary of the military department concerned for review as a superior authorized to exercise general court-martial convening authority. 
    (d) Review of Cases Not Referred to Court-martial Following Staff Judge Advocate Recommendation Not to Refer for Trial.—In any case where a staff judge advocate, pursuant to section 834 of title 10, United States Code (article 34 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice), recommends that charges of a sex-related offense should not be referred for trial by court-martial and the convening authority decides not to refer any charges to a court-martial, the convening authority shall forward the case file for review to the next superior commander authorized to exercise general court-martial convening authority. 
    (e) Elements of Case File.—A case file forwarded to higher authority for review pursuant to subsection (c) or (d) shall include the following:
        (1) All charges and specifications preferred under section 830 of title 10, United States Code (article 30 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice). 
        (2) All reports of investigations of such charges, including the military criminal investigative organization investigation report and the report prepared under section 832 of title 10, United States Code (article 32 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice), as amended by section 1702. 
        (3) A certification that the victim of the alleged sex-related offense was notified of the opportunity to express views on the victim’s preferred disposition of the alleged offense for consideration by the convening authority. 
        (4) All statements of the victim provided to the military criminal investigative organization and to the victim’s chain of command relating to the alleged sex-related offense and any statement provided by the victim to the convening authority 
expressing the victim’s view on the victim’s preferred disposition of the alleged offense. 
        (5) The written advice of the staff judge advocate to the convening authority pursuant to section 834 of title 10, United States Code (article 34 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice). 
        (6) A written statement explaining the reasons for the convening authority’s decision not to refer any charges for trial by court-martial. 
        (7) A certification that the victim of the alleged sex-related offense was informed of the convening authority’s decision to forward the case as provided in subsection (c) or (d).  
    (f) Notice on Results or Review.—The victim of the alleged sex-related offense shall be notified of the results of the review conducted under subsection (c) or (d) in the manner prescribed by the victims and witness assistance program of the Armed Force concerned. 
    (g) Victim Allegation of Sex-related Offense.—The Secretary of Defense shall require the Secretaries of the military departments to develop a system to ensure that a victim of a possible sex-related offense under the Uniform Code of Military Justice is given the opportunity to state, either at the time of making an unrestricted report of the allegation or during the criminal investigation of the allegation, whether or not the victim believes that the offense alleged is a sex-related offense subject to the requirements of this section.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the victim's opportunity to express views on the preferred disposition is outside consultation before a federal decision. But this is input into an individual, case-specific prosecutorial decision (whether to refer charges to court-martial), not a policy decision, and the victim is often a service member. The review mechanism itself runs entirely within the military chain of command (convening authority, staff judge advocate, superior commander, Secretary of the military department). There is no comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, consultation with outside entities, or right to sue.
fable.s: the convening authority shall forward the case file to the Secretary of the military department concerned for review as a superior authorized to exercise general court-martial convening authority

opus.w: The section sets up internal military review of individual decisions not to refer sex-offense charges to court-martial, and every reviewer is a federal official. The victim's chance to give views is input on how one criminal case is resolved. Like the manufacturer's opportunity to present views in Example 11, that is not participation in a federal policy decision. Many victims are also service members, so nobody clearly outside the federal government takes part in a policy decision.
opus.s: A certification that the victim of the alleged sex-related offense was notified of the opportunity to express views on the victim’s preferred disposition of the alleged offense for consideration by the convening authority.
opus.b:
1. **Tempting reading:** The section gives victims an "opportunity to express views" on how their case should be resolved, and requires the convening authority to consider those views. That looks like the government consulting someone before it decides.
2. **Why it fails:** The decision is whether to prosecute one person, not a policy decision. Example 11 treats a party's chance to present views in an individual enforcement case as not participation. Every reviewer here is inside the federal government: the convening authority, staff judge advocates, superior commanders and the Secretaries. Most victims under the Uniform Code of Military Justice are themselves service members. The only outside-facing parts are notices to the victim and the victim stating their views in their own case. Some victims could be civilians, so this is a close call.

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines procedural rights for victims within the military justice system, specifically requiring that their statements be considered during internal reviews of prosecutorial decisions. This is a due process right for an individual party in a specific case, not a mechanism for public participation in federal policy or administrative decision-making (such as advisory committees, public comment periods, or consultation with states/tribes). The definition of participation focuses on broader consultation or coordination with outside entities before federal actions, whereas this is a specific legal requirement for case handling.
qwen_chat.s: consideration be given to the victim’s statement provided during the course of the criminal investigation regarding the alleged sex-related offense perpetrated against the victim
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the victim (a private citizen) is allowed to provide a statement and have their views considered in the decision-making process regarding whether to refer charges for trial, this constitutes "participation" as defined (consultation with people outside the government before making a decision). The text explicitly requires that the victim's statement and views be considered.

Why it fails: The definition of participation focuses on the federal government consulting with outsiders *before* making a decision in a regulatory, policy, or administrative context (like rulemaking, grants, or advisory boards). This section describes a specific procedural right within the military justice system (Uniform Code of Military Justice) for a victim of a crime to be heard during an internal administrative review of a prosecutorial decision. While the victim is outside the government, this is a due process/rights provision within a specific legal proceeding rather than a general mechanism for public participation in federal decision-making (like a public comment period or advisory committee). More importantly, the "decision" here is a prosecutorial discretion decision within the military chain of command, and the "participation" is limited to providing a statement for consideration, which is often categorized as a victim's right rather than "public participation" in the statutory sense intended by the definition (which emphasizes advisory boards, comment periods, and consultation with states/tribes/experts for policy decisions). However, looking closer at the definition: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." The victim is outside the government. The government (convening authority) makes a decision (whether to refer charges). The government *must* consider the victim's views. This fits the literal definition. BUT, the "No" traps include "applications for benefits" and "intra-government coordination". Is this intra-government? No, the victim is outside. Is it an application? No. Is it a right to sue? No.

Let's re-read the "No" traps carefully. "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision."

Let's look at the "Yes" criteria: "consultation or coordination with states, tribes, local governments, or other outside entities before a federal action". The victim is an "other outside entity". The action is "referral for trial". The government must consider the victim's views.

However, often in these legal labeling tasks, "participation" refers to *policy* or *regulatory* participation, not individual case adjudication rights. The definition says "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." It doesn't restrict it to policy. But the examples given are "advisory board", "comment period", "public hearing". These are broad, multi-party mechanisms. This section is about a specific victim in a specific case.

Let's look at the "Tempting-but-wrong" pattern in previous examples.
Example 3: Consultation with experts for a study -> No (not a decision).
Example 5: Agreement with union in past -> No (past).
Example 6: Board members are employees -> No.
Example 7: Advisory board determines emblems -> Yes.

In this case, the victim's input is part of the *case file* for review. It is a procedural right. Is it "participation"? The definition is broad. "Consult or coordinate... before making a decision." The convening authority considers the victim's views. This is consultation.

However, there is a strong argument that this is *not* participation in the sense of the definition because it is a *right* of the victim within a legal process, not a *mechanism* for public input into government policy. The definition's examples (advisory boards, comment periods) are mechanisms for *general* input. This is *specific* input for a *specific* case.

Let's look at the "No" trap: "applications for benefits... applying for something is not participating". This is similar to applying for a specific outcome in a legal case.

Actually, the most likely intended answer is **No**. Why? Because the "participation" definition in this context usually refers to *democratic* or *administrative* participation in *policy* or *program* decisions, not individual due process rights in criminal proceedings. The victim is a party to the case, not a "participant" in the government's decision-making process in the sense of an advisory role or public comment. The government isn't "consulting" the victim to get their opinion on a policy; it is legally required to consider their statement as part of the evidence/procedure.

Let's try to find a reason for "Yes". The definition says "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision." This implies that legal rights can be participation. But this isn't suing. It's providing a statement.

Let's look at the "No" trap: "intra-government coordination". This is not intra-government.

Let's look at the "Yes" criteria: "consultation or coordination with... other outside entities".

I will lean towards **No** because this is a specific procedural right in a criminal justice context, not a general participation mechanism like a public hearing or advisory committee. The "participation" label is typically reserved for broader engagement mechanisms.
